title: General recommendation No. 36 (2020) on preventing and combating racial profiling by law enforcement officials | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that racial profiling by law enforcement violates international human rights law, that determinations should rest on objective criteria and individual conduct rather than group membership, and that algorithmic profiling can deepen discriminatory policing.

title: Preventing and countering racial profiling of people of African descent (2019) | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that racial profiling relies on generalizations instead of objective evidence or individual behaviour, burdens equality, liberty, privacy, movement, and protection against arbitrary intervention, and should be replaced by prohibition, accountability, and better law-enforcement practice.

title: A/HRC/60/75: Systemic racism against Africans and people of African descent in the criminal justice system | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that racial discrimination permeates all layers of the criminal justice system, including through racial profiling and arbitrary deprivation of liberty, and that initiation-stage discrimination is tied to later detention and conviction burdens.

title: Joint general recommendation No. 38 (2025) on general guidelines for eradicating xenophobia towards migrants and others perceived as such | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that migration-linked and perceived-foreignness targeting belongs inside the archive's anti-profiling surface and that public policy must address xenophobia toward migrants and others perceived as such rather than treating it as outside ordinary equality law.

title: Human Rights at International Borders: A Trainer’s Guide | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that watch lists and no-fly lists may lack due process and oversight, that unjustified inclusion can violate privacy and freedom of movement, and that transparency, correction, and appeal must accompany watchlist use.

title: Basic Human Rights Reference Guide: Right to a Fair Trial and Due Process in the Context of Countering Terrorism | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that due process applies across criminal, administrative, and expulsion contexts in counter-terrorism settings, and that listed or otherwise affected persons require review, representation, and effective remedy rather than mere administrative designation.

title: Basic Human Rights Reference Guide on Proscription of Organizations in the Context of Countering Terrorism | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that proscription and related listing decisions affecting organizations and associated individuals must be legally bounded and effectively challengeable, including challenge to the legality and effects of the decision.

title: Security Council’s counter-terrorism measures lack legal basis, says UN expert | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that due-process rights remain at stake in terrorist listing and delisting systems and that listed individuals and entities should have access to domestic courts to challenge implementing measures and national terrorist lists.

title: UN Security Council / Al-Qaida sanctions regime: UN rights expert sounds alarm at delisting procedures | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that list inclusion can seriously interfere with freedom of movement, property, and privacy; that judicial review was lacking; and that delisting without disclosure, decision power, or funded legal presentation falls short of due-process standards.

title: A/HRC/22/28: Report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that organizing a protest should not be subject to prior authorization, but at most to a notification procedure, and that assemblies should be approached under a presumption in favour of holding them.

title: A/HRC/23/39: Report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that the formation of associations should not be subject to prior authorization, that notification should be simple and non-onerous, and that peaceful assembly should likewise not require authorization.

title: Statement by Maina Kiai, United Nations Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, at the conclusion of his visit to Chile | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claim that requiring authorization turns the right to freedom of peaceful assembly into a privilege and that prior notification, not prior permission, is the best-practice default.

title: Joint Declaration on Protecting the right to freedom of association from stigmatization in the face of “foreign agent” and similar initiatives | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that registered and unregistered associations may seek and use resources without prior authorization, that restrictions must be case-specific and evidence-based, and that states should not compel associations to register in order to exist and operate freely.

title: A/HRC/50/23: Access to resources - Report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, Clément Nyaletsossi Voule | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that access to resources belongs inside freedom of association and that states may not use funding-origin rhetoric or broad transparency pretexts to differentially burden civic actors without rights-disciplined justification.

title: A/HRC/53/38/Add.4: General principles and guidelines on ensuring the right of civil society organizations to have access to resources | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that states should maintain an enabling environment for civil society organizations to access resources and that differential treatment tied to foreign origin or similar suspicion should not displace non-discrimination, proportionality, and review.

title: A/79/263: Protecting the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association from stigmatization - Report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association, Gina Romero | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that negative and stigmatizing rhetoric directed at civil society and activists harms the effective enjoyment of assembly and association and that states must prevent and counter such narratives rather than institutionalize them.

title: Bosnia and Herzegovina: Bill on registering NGOs will increase government control over civil society operations, say UN experts | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that foreign-funding registry schemes can impose severe restrictions, increase government control over NGOs, and stigmatize civil society through pejorative foreign-agent style designation.

title: El Salvador: Concerns over Foreign Agents law | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that foreign-agent laws can combine stigmatizing registration with special taxes, fines, and penalties that threaten civil society activity and chill human-rights work.

title: A/HRC/20/27: Report of the Special Rapporteur on the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and of association | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that access to funding and resources is an integral and vital part of freedom of association and that registered and unregistered associations should be able to seek resources from domestic, foreign, and international sources without prior approval.

title: Best Practices on Combating the Abuse of Non-Profit Organisations | FATF
why_used: Used for the claims that FATF's revised risk-based approach should protect relevant non-profits without unduly disrupting or discouraging legitimate activities and that overly burdensome or restrictive controls are bad practice.

title: Guidance Note on Overcompliance with Unilateral Sanctions and its Harmful Effects on Human Rights | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that excessive risk avoidance can block authorized transactions, impose onerous documentation, charge discouraging fees, create long delays, freeze assets not actually targeted, and deny access to bank accounts, illuminating financial-chokepoint governance beyond formal prohibition.

title: Bachelet dismayed at restrictions on human rights NGOs and arrests of activists in India | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that bank-account freezes can force human-rights organizations to close offices and halt work, showing how formal legality can be hollowed out by financial disablement.

title: Uganda: UN experts urge stronger human rights safeguards ahead of 2026 elections | OHCHR
why_used: Used for the claims that freezing of bank accounts can operate as an arbitrary barrier against civil society alongside permit delays and surveillance, especially in politically charged periods.
